constraints: The opportunity depends on discovering new paths in a changing corpus.
Citations, budget limits, and human review are required before action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The evaluated pilot costs more and may leave findings pending review, but it tests the transformational hypothesis without making exploration an uncontrolled action path.
details.errorCorrection: Match transformation claims to a measurable capability and preserve a review boundary for uncertain or consequential findings.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An agent can choose follow-up searches as findings change; budgets, source records, evaluation cases, and a human gate constrain the exploratory path.
details.scenarioApplication: Measure discovery recall, citation support, time, spend, and reviewer acceptance on representative research tasks before expanding the pilot.
details.transfer: For high-upside discovery, define the evidence, budget, and human decision boundary as part of the value case rather than as post-launch cleanup.

messages.text: A fixed path may be efficient but cannot adapt to the discovery-dependent work described and would publish without the required review.
Unrestricted exploration lacks a spending and evidence boundary and crosses the human action requirement.
Document count is an activity measure; it does not establish a useful discovery or supported conclusion.

feedback.reason: Open-ended discovery is where adaptive exploration can create transformational value, but the pilot needs evidence, stop conditions, and human ownership before action.

options.text: Use a fixed retrieval workflow and publish its first answer as the discovery result so cost and latency remain predictable.
Open the full corpus to an unrestricted agent and let it act on a novel finding without an evidence or spending boundary.
Pilot an evaluated agentic research path with bounded searches, source citations, cost tracking, and human review of the proposed conclusion.
Optimize only the number of documents searched and treat broad corpus coverage as transformation regardless of finding quality.

prompt: A research group seeks potentially transformational discovery across a changing corpus. Exploration is open-ended and a human must review evidence before any conclusion is acted on. Which value-aligned design should be piloted?

constraints: Completion is high but does not reflect reviewer effort or outcome quality.
The current process can provide a baseline for resolution and handling time.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Richer measurement requires labeling and instrumentation, but it distinguishes a valuable draft from a fluent draft that adds work.
details.errorCorrection: Measure the business process end to end, including human correction, rather than optimizing a model-output or completion counter.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Resolution and acceptance capture usefulness, while handling time and rework capture productivity; segmentation shows where the assistant helps or burdens agents.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare accepted answers, resolution and repeat contacts, minutes per case, and edits with a matched baseline before changing prompts or models.
details.transfer: Whenever a product metric stays high while users still work around the system, add outcome and effort measures tied to the current process.

messages.text: Raising a proxy threshold does not address the unchanged handling time or reveal whether conversations actually resolve.
Generated volume can increase editing burden and says nothing about acceptance or customer outcome.
Rewriting identifies a possible defect but not whether a targeted prompt, route, or workflow change could recover value.

feedback.reason: Completion is a weak proxy when human rewriting consumes the supposed time benefit. The next diagnosis must measure the actual work and outcome against current practice.

options.text: Increase the completion target to 98% and treat the higher percentage as proof that the assistant creates productivity.
Measure resolution, accepted-answer rate, handling time, and rework against the current process, segmented by conversation type.
Count generated words and use longer answers as evidence that the assistant addresses more customer needs.
Replace the model immediately because any rewriting means the AI path has no business value.

prompt: A dashboard reports that 92% of conversations completed, but agents spend the same time because they rewrite many answers before sending them. Which measurement diagnosis should guide the next change?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Draft volume ignores whether reviewers can use the output without rework.
details.errorCorrection: Using the strongest route for all traffic may add cost where a simpler path is sufficient.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Model selection should be tested against use-case criteria and weighed by completed-task cost.
details.scenarioApplication: The legal slice has a material quality floor; token price alone does not prove it is met.
details.transfer: Compare cost per acceptable completed task and keep required quality and service constraints visible by slice.

messages.text: Lowest per-token price can still fail the legal clause requirement or create costly corrections.
Strongest-for-all assumes every workload needs the same capability and ignores the stated production cost.
A larger draft count is not business value if outputs require correction.

feedback.reason: The business outcome is an acceptable completed notice, not an inexpensive token or a large draft count. Segmenting routine and legal work can reveal whether one model meets each slice’s quality and cost needs.

options.text: Choose the model with the lowest price per token for every notice.
Compare cost per acceptable notice by type, including quality floors and reviewer time.
Choose the highest-quality model for every notice because reviewer time has no cost.
Measure total tokens and maximize the number of drafts, regardless of acceptance or correction work.

prompt: A translation team pays per generated token, and a costly model returns excellent drafts. Reviewers find that routine notices require only simple rewrites, while a smaller set of legal notices needs nuanced clause preservation. Which value-aligned test should guide allocation?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Removing source evidence weakens the condition that makes the research result useful.
details.errorCorrection: A blended average can hide failures against the routine SLA.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Success criteria can include separate quality and latency dimensions for different workload slices.
details.scenarioApplication: Only the condition with measured research value takes the slower route.
details.transfer: Use per-slice routing when a slower capability creates value only for an identifiable exception class.

messages.text: The measured improvement is limited to conflicts, so making every routine request wait adds latency without matching value.
The routine path still must meet its explicit 1.5-second requirement.
The conflict case needs evidence; removing the citation requirement evades the quality need.

feedback.reason: The valuable slower path applies only to an evidence conflict, while the ordinary path has a hard response contract. Routing preserves both service expectations and makes the exception state visible.

options.text: Keep routine answers within SLA; route conflicts to research with a pending state and separate measure.
Run research for every question and ask dispatchers to tolerate the latency because the research answers are better.
Set one average latency target across both paths so the slower conflict cases do not appear as outliers.
Remove the manual citation requirement from conflict cases to preserve the 1.5-second target.

prompt: A dispatch assistant must return a usable answer within 1.5 seconds for routine questions. A high-quality research path takes 8 seconds and materially improves only cases where an asset record conflicts with the manual. What design best aligns the SLA and quality value?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tool count measures capability breadth, not business value or service outcomes.
details.errorCorrection: The predictable majority does not rule out a model for the distinct investigative task.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Simplicity is appropriate for predictable work; added agentic complexity needs evidence of value.
details.scenarioApplication: The exception slice is where the decision structure differs and should be measured separately.
details.transfer: Align architecture to the work distribution, then compare incremental value against the existing baseline.

messages.text: A single open-ended path imposes extra cost and variability on routine requests without evidence that they benefit.
The 8% evidence-dependent slice may benefit from a bounded investigation path.
More tools do not prove the service changed user outcomes.

feedback.reason: The case has a stable majority and a smaller workload with genuinely variable steps. A targeted pilot tests whether autonomy adds value for that slice without changing a routine path that already meets its service target.

options.text: Replace all cases with an open-ended agent to maximize the amount of work done by Claude.
Do not use Claude anywhere because most cases are predictable.
Measure the number of tools the agent can call as evidence of transformation.
Keep routine workflow; test investigation on the 8% exception slice.

prompt: A product executive wants a “transformational agent” for a workflow. A study finds that 92% of requests follow the same three steps, while 8% require unplanned investigation; the current queue already meets its service target for routine requests. Which value proposal is strongest?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Final review alone is not an adequate plan when the missed field can cause irreversible loss.
details.errorCorrection: The case supports a targeted safeguard and evaluation, not a claim that all extraction is useless.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Success measures need to reflect material task-specific risks, not just averages.
details.scenarioApplication: The rare deadline field needs its own requirement and an explicit uncertainty path.
details.transfer: Segment by consequence as well as frequency, and evaluate the full cost of controls.

messages.text: The 99% aggregate does not reveal the deadline-field recall or the consequence of its misses.
The observed weakness is concentrated in one field and can be addressed with a targeted gate.
Relying on discovery at final review does not prevent a missed statutory deadline.

feedback.reason: Aggregate accuracy hides a low-recall, high-consequence slice. The decision must protect deadline recall and include the human review cost when evaluating productivity.

options.text: Expand broadly because average accuracy and staff time both improved.
Stop all automation because one field is occasionally missed.
Require deadline-field recall; review uncertain cases and count that work.
Optimize extraction speed and let staff discover missed deadlines during final review.

prompt: A case-management assistant reports 99% field extraction accuracy on ordinary cases. A separate high-impact slice contains rare deadline fields; 12% are missed, and missing one can forfeit an appeal. Overall staff time fell by 15%. What should guide expansion?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An aggregate score can obscure which configuration meets the stated requirement and where it improves.
details.errorCorrection: A higher score on an optional slice does not establish that the compliant alternative is unsafe.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Cost and capability should be compared against the actual task requirements and workload slices.
details.scenarioApplication: The routine requirement is met at lower cost; the exception slice has no current quality floor.
details.transfer: Revisit routing when required outcomes, error consequences, or workload distribution change.

messages.text: Higher raw performance has no stated business value for this optional slice under the current contract.
The case says the routine path meets its floor, and the exception result is not currently required.
A blended score hides that both meet routine requirements while only one changes an optional slice.

feedback.reason: Both configurations meet the required routine floor, and the measured incremental gain applies to an explicitly optional slice. The lower-cost route satisfies the current contract; the decision should change if that slice becomes required or its volume/consequence changes.

options.text: Use the stronger configuration everywhere because a higher score is always more valuable.
Use the cheaper compliant route until exception need or volume changes.
Use the stronger configuration because its improvement proves the faster one is unsafe.
Average both configurations’ metrics and pick whichever has the better combined score.

prompt: A service chooses between two Claude configurations for routine invoice extraction. On 10,000 representative invoices, both exceed the required field-accuracy floor; the faster configuration costs 40% less, while the stronger configuration improves a rare exception slice that the business has classified as optional for this workflow. What is the strongest decision?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Acceptance can be a useful diagnostic but does not replace the business metric named in the case.
details.errorCorrection: A faster initial reply does not establish a net reduction in staff time per resolved case.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Productivity must be measured across the complete work needed to resolve a case.
details.scenarioApplication: The pilot saves two minutes at first response but adds 3.5 minutes of correction and follow-up to the stated target.
details.transfer: Compare end-to-end time and outcome quality before treating a workflow pilot as productive.

messages.text: First-response time omits the added correction and follow-up effort in the stated target.
Acceptance is an activity or proxy and may not capture the staff time cost described.
The evidence does not show model capacity caused the rework or that a stronger model would eliminate it.

feedback.reason: The target is total staff time per resolved case. The 2-minute first response is offset by 3.5 minutes of correction and follow-up, so the pilot has not demonstrated the required productivity improvement.

options.text: Do not claim a productivity gain from first-response speed; measure total staff time and address the added correction work before expansion.
Expand because the first response is twice as fast.
Use answer acceptance instead of total time because it is easier to collect.
Route all cases to the strongest model to guarantee the correction work disappears.

prompt: A contact-center pilot cuts average first-response time from 4 minutes to 2 minutes, but adds 3.5 minutes of average correction and follow-up work per case. Resolution rate is unchanged, and the productivity target is total staff time per resolved case. What conclusion follows?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A narrower document class could be evaluated if it has a distinct error profile and the contract permits that scope.
details.errorCorrection: Optimizing a weighted average without honoring a hard threshold can produce an unusable system.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Business value is constrained by explicit quality and service guardrails as well as efficiency.
details.scenarioApplication: The measured 1.1% error rate exceeds the 0.3% contractual maximum, even though unit cost falls.
details.transfer: Treat hard limits as feasibility constraints before optimizing cost, speed, or volume.

messages.text: A future correction budget does not change the stated quality ceiling or prove the economics after correction.
Customer reports are late and incomplete evidence for a known contractual error limit.
The contract sets a 0.3% maximum; an unrelated 2% threshold does not satisfy it.

feedback.reason: Cost and throughput gains do not compensate for missing a binding quality limit. The architecture must first meet the critical-field ceiling or define a permitted lower-risk subset.

options.text: Adopt it because the lower unit cost can fund later correction work.
Adopt it for all documents and let customers report mistakes.
Meet the critical-field floor first, then remeasure cost or narrow the eligible scope.
Compare only the total number of documents processed because the error rate is below 2%.

prompt: A data-entry assistant lowers cost per document by 18%, but the pilot’s critical-field error rate rises from 0.2% to 1.1%. The contractual maximum is 0.3%; staff time and throughput improve. What is the decision?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the retry path is necessary for quality, the team may need to renegotiate latency or change the workflow; that tradeoff must be explicit.
details.errorCorrection: A lower average cannot demonstrate that a p95 SLA is met.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Performance value must be evaluated against the exact latency statistic and threshold promised to users.
details.scenarioApplication: The new mean improves, but p95 remains 0.7 seconds above the limit and a specific class accounts for repeated retries.
details.transfer: Report percentile metrics and slices that drive the tail, then evaluate targeted mitigations against quality and cost.

messages.text: The contract is p95, not mean latency; the reported percentile still fails.
A longer timeout can worsen the measured tail and does not address why retries occur.
The evidence identifies retries in one document class, not insufficient reasoning capability for all requests.

feedback.reason: The target is a tail percentile, and the measured p95 remains over its limit. Diagnose the retry-heavy slice rather than treating an improved mean as success.

options.text: Diagnose the retry-heavy slice; the measured p95 still misses the SLA.
It meets the SLA because the average is below 2 seconds.
Increase the timeout for all requests so the slow tail can finish successfully.
Switch every request to a more capable model, since the tail must be a reasoning problem.

prompt: A recommendation service reduces mean latency from 3.1 seconds to 1.2 seconds. The business target is p95 under 2 seconds; the new p95 is 2.7 seconds because a small document class triggers repeated retries. Which value assessment is sound?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the review is needed only on high-risk cases, measure those cases separately and include their actual share.
details.errorCorrection: Multiplying gross savings by every query overstates value by ignoring the baseline mix and added labor.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Business value compares the whole current and proposed workflow, weighted by actual workload and costs.
details.scenarioApplication: The 30-second gross saving can be overwhelmed by 45 seconds of review and should apply only to queries that previously incurred lookup effort.
details.transfer: Use net outcomes by relevant workload slice; do not substitute model speed or acceptance for business benefit.

messages.text: The gross saving ignores review effort and counts queries that had no lookup baseline.
Response latency alone does not include whether people spend less total time completing the work.
Acceptance is useful quality evidence but not a measure of net labor or service outcomes.

feedback.reason: The gross lookup reduction does not account for the new review step or queries that already required no lookup. A case-mix-aware end-to-end estimate is needed.

options.text: Compare net time by query type, including baseline work, review, escalations, and adoption.
Multiply the gross 30-second reduction by total weekly volume, then subtract review time from a small sample.
Measure model response latency because shorter responses are the direct source of productivity.
Report only the percentage of answers accepted by reviewers.

prompt: An internal search assistant reduces average lookup time by 30 seconds, but the new workflow requires a reviewer to spend 45 seconds checking every answer. Search volume is 4,000 per week; 25% of queries currently need no human lookup. Which calculation is most useful for the business case?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a controlled route can meet the error floor and staff the review slice, a staged expansion may be justified with explicit monitoring.
details.errorCorrection: A half rollout still creates queue load and does not establish that the contractual quality floor is met.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Value optimization is constrained by quality floors and operational capacity; lower model cost alone is insufficient.
details.scenarioApplication: The review rate more than doubles while the team is at capacity, and the unresolved-error ceiling is a hard requirement.
details.transfer: Treat contractual floors and service capacity as constraints before optimizing cost.

messages.text: Inference savings do not establish total cost or compliance with the unresolved-error limit.
Reducing traffic does not make the known review-capacity gap disappear, and the answer offers no gate for the error limit.
Lower latency cannot by itself resolve capacity or routing correctness.

feedback.reason: The cost reduction cannot offset a breached service constraint or unstaffed review demand. Evaluate quality and operational capacity before expanding, then compare total cost.

options.text: Roll out because inference savings are certain while future labor costs are hard to estimate.
Limit rollout to half the traffic and monitor whether the new review queue stays manageable.
Gate rollout on staffed review capacity and the 0.5% error cap, then compare total cost.
Choose the lowest-latency model so more cases can move through review.

prompt: A document-routing pilot lowers inference cost by 22%. It also increases manual review from 8% to 19%; the review team is already at capacity, and the contract caps unresolved routing errors at 0.5%. Which rollout decision follows the stated value constraints?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the owner changes the exception floor, document the revised risk decision before comparing costs.
details.errorCorrection: Applying a 4% weight to the floor turns a slice-level requirement into an aggregate that can hide misses.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Separate non-negotiable slice floors from workload-weighted cost and labor estimates.
details.scenarioApplication: A low-volume exception group still has an explicit 98% recall floor.
details.transfer: Use slice-specific quality gates and workload-aware economic analysis together.

messages.text: The scenario requires 98% exception recall; a review queue is not evidence that the model/system meets it.
Traffic share can weight aggregate workload but cannot relax the stated within-slice floor.
Average review time does not establish that the 98% recall constraint is met.

feedback.reason: The exception quality floor is a constraint, while costs and review load can be weighted by actual workload for business value. One aggregate should not erase a required slice minimum.

options.text: Prioritize routine cost because it dominates volume, then handle exception misses through the existing review queue.
Check the exception recall floor separately; estimate total cost and review labor using the real case mix.
Weight the 98% recall target by the 4% exception share when judging total-system recall.
Choose the route with lowest average review time, then monitor exception outcomes after launch.

prompt: A route table from a two-week pilot shows model cost per case: routine $0.01, exception $0.03. Human review takes 20 seconds on 5% of routine cases and 4 minutes on 35% of exception cases. Exception volume is only 4%, but these cases have a 98% recall floor. Which evaluation statement is sound?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the statutory deadline applies only to a subset, define the routing trigger and measure false negatives as part of the system.
details.errorCorrection: Overall latency can hide a concentrated failure in a high-consequence segment.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Performance and quality service objectives may impose slice-specific hard constraints before cost optimization.
details.scenarioApplication: Route A breaches the urgent deadline that protects a statutory outcome.
details.transfer: Tie workload segmentation to business consequences and explicit service criteria.

messages.text: The mix average can hide the urgent-call breach tied to statutory deadlines.
Routine performance does not resolve the urgent slice with a statutory consequence.
The statutory consequence makes this more than an optional cost preference; the required service constraint must be established.

feedback.reason: The urgent slice has a consequence-bearing deadline. Its low volume does not make an average or cost comparison sufficient.

options.text: Use overall latency because it reflects the actual mix and gives one comparable deployment target.
Compare unit cost first because Route A meets the target for 99% of routine calls.
Check urgent-call volume and ask the owner whether a separate deadline target is worth the cost.
Treat the urgent SLA as its own gate; compare costs only among routes that meet it.

prompt: A dispatch assistant has two candidate routes. Route A meets the 1-second p95 target for 99% of routine calls but breaches it on urgent calls; Route B meets it on both groups at higher cost. Urgent calls are 7% of traffic and failure can miss a statutory deadline. What should the architect compare?

constraints: The measured speed gain is paired with a material resolution regression.
The target resolution floor is 82% and slices can be evaluated before broad rollout.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Expansion pauses and analysis costs time, but it avoids scaling a fast workflow that drives repeat contacts and damages service value.
details.errorCorrection: Treat speed and outcome quality as a joint business constraint and use failure slices to target the smallest corrective change.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Segmented evaluation can locate failure classes such as policy gaps or unsafe confidence; routing, prompt, retrieval, or review changes can then be tested against both SLA pillars.
details.scenarioApplication: Hold broad rollout, compare resolution and handle time by intent and customer segment, and accept a revised path only when it clears the 82% floor without unacceptable effort.
details.transfer: When efficiency improves while outcome quality falls, keep both measures in the gate and diagnose the work slice before choosing rollout or redesign.

messages.text: Handle time alone ignores the resolution target and accepts a workflow that shifts effort into repeat contacts.
A full permanent rollback discards potentially recoverable value before identifying whether one slice or route causes the regression.
Changing the target hides a measured failure instead of bringing the service back to the agreed business floor.

feedback.reason: A faster interaction that fails to resolve the contact misses the service value target. The next step is a slice diagnosis and measured revision, not a single-metric rollout or an unscoped permanent rollback.

options.text: Keep the release because handle-time improvement is the clearest efficiency signal, and address repeat contacts after adoption grows.
Roll back every AI feature permanently because one aggregate outcome regressed without testing where the regression occurs.
Pause broad expansion, segment the resolution failures, and retest a scoped prompt, retrieval, or human route until the 82% floor and acceptable handling time are jointly met.
Raise the resolution target in the dashboard to match the observed result while continuing the same design.

prompt: A contact-center assistant reduces average handle time by 18%, but first-contact resolution falls from 84% to 72% and repeat contacts increase. The target is at least 82% first-contact resolution. What decision should follow?

constraints: The current evidence covers acceptance but not operational or downstream value.
Broader deployment can wait for a defined measurement gate.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A longer pilot delays scale and requires outcome follow-up, but it protects the insurer from optimizing summaries that save no time or alter claim quality adversely.
details.errorCorrection: Do not turn early approval into a broad productivity claim; define the operational and downstream measures before increasing exposure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A pilot can connect summary versions to adjuster behavior, decision time, corrections, and later claim outcomes, producing a balanced value evaluation.
details.scenarioApplication: Instrument representative adjusters and claim slices, compare with current practice, and expand only if quality remains acceptable while time and downstream outcomes improve.
details.transfer: For AI features with indirect business effects, measure adoption, effort, corrections, and downstream outcomes before calling a pilot successful.

messages.text: Acceptance does not establish adoption, time-to-decision, correction burden, or downstream claim quality at scale.
Token cost is one constraint and cannot replace the quality and operational measures needed for the business decision.
Generation volume measures activity, not whether adjusters use the summaries or whether claims resolve better.

feedback.reason: Acceptance is useful but incomplete. The business case concerns adoption, time, correction burden, and claim outcomes, so expansion needs a measurement gate for those effects.

options.text: Extend the pilot with measures for adjuster adoption, time-to-decision, correction rate, and downstream outcomes, then gate expansion on predefined thresholds.
Expand to every adjuster because acceptance of the summaries proves that the insurer will realize productivity value.
Stop measuring and select the model with the lowest token cost so the pilot cannot exceed budget.
Use the number of summaries generated as the expansion criterion and infer claim quality from coverage.

prompt: An insurer pilots Claude summaries for adjusters. Managers want broader deployment, but the pilot has only summary acceptance data; adoption, time-to-decision, correction rate, and downstream claim outcomes were not measured. What value decision is appropriate?

constraints: The efficient model scores 91% and the stronger model 98% on the same held-out exception set.
At least 97% recall of material exceptions is required.
High-impact appeals are a minority and a human path remains available; the stronger route meets the asynchronous deadline.
The high-impact exception-review workload is identified by authoritative caseworker intake before model routing; the efficient model is not used to detect which appeals contain exceptions.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the efficient model cleared 97% on the same held-out slice, use it as the default and test a stronger route only for measured residual failures.
details.errorCorrection: The efficient path misses the material-exception floor and shifts error cost into appeals without meeting the business outcome.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends evaluating model capabilities, speed, cost, and effort against the actual use case rather than optimizing one dimension alone. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The material-exception quality floor is a hard business requirement, so efficiency cannot justify a path that fails it.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the stronger model for the exception workload or route it to a validated stronger or human path, and retain the efficient model only where its measured quality clears the applicable floor.
details.transfer: Route slices against held-out quality floors, using the costlier model or a validated human path only where the efficient route fails the required outcome.

messages.text: The efficient path misses the material-exception floor and shifts error cost into appeals without meeting the business outcome.
The stronger model clears the exception floor, but applying its four-times unit cost to every case ignores the stated minority workload and available allocation boundary.
Random sampling does not ensure the material-exception slice clears 97%; the measured failure is already known and should drive the route.

feedback.reason: Value alignment can favor higher capability when a consequence-bearing quality floor is explicit and the route remains operationally feasible.

options.text: Use the efficient model for all appeals because its lower cost maximizes productivity.
Use the stronger model for every appeal because quality is hard, and defer any cost or workload segmentation review.
Use the stronger route for exception cases, keeping the efficient model only where its measured quality clears the floor.
Route a random quarter of appeals to the stronger model and accept efficient output for the rest until an incident identifies a quality problem.

prompt:
A tax-appeal assistant must recall at least 97% of material exceptions. The efficient model reaches 91%, while a stronger model reaches 98% at four times the unit cost and remains under the asynchronous service deadline.

Which model allocation satisfies the material-exception quality requirement?

constraints: Both models were measured on the same routine and high-impact classes.
The high-impact floor is 95%, the service p95 limit is 2.5 seconds, and the monthly model budget is $2,500.
Classifier uncertainty has a reviewer path; the measured segmented route costs $2,300 and the stronger model is used for 10,000 high-impact cases.

A production-shaped replay of the segmented route, including classifier and orchestration overhead, measures end-to-end p95 at 2.4 seconds. Uncertain classifications return a pending acknowledgment within the same limit; a separate approved reviewer workflow holds any consequential action until resolution.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the stronger route measured above 2.5 seconds end to end under the routed load, reject that route for the hard-deadline slice and use a reviewed asynchronous or narrower escalation path; if its cost fell below the global budget, broaden only after the same class gates pass.
details.errorCorrection: All-stronger costs $7,500 and exceeds the $2,500 model budget; all-efficient scores91% on the high-impact slice and fails its95% floor. The production-shaped segmented replay, including routing overhead, measures2.4 seconds p95; model-only2.3-second timing alone would not establish that result.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends evaluating model capabilities, speed, cost, and effort against the actual use case rather than optimizing one dimension alone. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Both models were measured on the same classes, so the decision must satisfy the 95% high-impact floor, 2.5-second p95 limit, and $2,500 monthly budget together.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the efficient model for the validated routine slice and the stronger model for the high-impact slice. The measured end-to-end route meets 2.5 seconds p95 and costs $2,300; uncertain classifications acknowledge pending and hold consequential action for the approved reviewer path.
details.transfer: Validate routing against slice quality, end-to-end latency, total budget, and the uncertain-case hold path together; model-only timing does not establish service feasibility.

messages.text: The efficient model scores only 91% on high-impact cases, below the 95% hard floor, so its lower cost cannot justify an all-efficient route.
The all-stronger route costs $7,500 per month and exceeds the $2,500 budget even though its latency and quality are acceptable.
Classifier precision and predicted classes do not replace end-to-end slice quality; unresolved high-impact uncertainty needs the bounded reviewer path.

feedback.reason: The worked monthly costs and same-class outcomes make segmented routing the only stated design that meets the high-impact floor without exceeding budget or latency.

options.text: Use the efficient model for all 50,000 cases because its $1,000 monthly cost is lowest.
Use the stronger model for every case because its 96% high-impact score clears the quality floor.
Route every case solely from the classifier, send no uncertainty cases to review, and accept the predicted class as the quality measure.
Route routine cases to the efficient model and high-impact cases to the stronger model, with budget, p95, quality, and reviewer gates.

prompt:
A claims triage service handles 50,000 cases per month: 40,000 routine and 10,000 high-impact cases. On the same held-out routine and high-impact classes, the efficient model scores 97% and 91%, costs $0.02 per case, and runs at 1.2 seconds p95; the stronger model scores 98% and 96%, costs $0.15, and runs at 2.3 seconds p95.

Which model route satisfies the shared quality, latency, budget, and uncertainty constraints?

constraints: The service has a latency and unit-cost target.
Both candidates need task-quality evidence and staff escalation remains available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The default path may automate fewer difficult cases, but it protects SLA and budget while generating evidence for a targeted upgrade.
details.errorCorrection: Align the architecture to the business value pillars and measured constraints instead of treating autonomy or price as a proxy for value.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A workload-specific benchmark links model pattern to latency, spend, quality, and escalation; the route makes a human or stronger path available where the efficient path is insufficient.
details.scenarioApplication: Measure answer correctness, p95, cost per question, and escalation on routine and difficult slices before setting the efficient path as the default.
details.transfer: When choosing among AI designs, compare task quality, speed, spend, and operational workload on the slice that creates the proposed value.

messages.text: Transformation language does not override a measured SLA and cost failure, and it provides no evidence that the extra autonomy helps the product-question task.
Price alone cannot establish useful answer quality or a safe default for customers.
Duplicate execution adds cost and answer length is not a business outcome or correctness measure.

feedback.reason: The efficient design meets the stated performance and cost constraints, but quality still needs evidence. Routing difficult cases preserves service value without paying the agentic cost for routine traffic.

options.text: Choose the agentic design because more autonomous steps signal greater transformation even though its measured latency and cost miss the target.
Choose the efficient design solely from price and skip quality measurement because retrieval is already familiar.
Run both designs for every customer and let answer length determine which one creates more value.
Use the efficient candidate for routine questions, verify its quality on representative cases, and route measured uncertainty or difficult cases to staff or a stronger path.

prompt: A retailer compares two designs for product questions. An efficient retrieval workflow measures 1.8 seconds p95 and meets the unit-cost budget; an agentic workflow measures 6.4 seconds p95 and exceeds it. Which initial decision aligns the solution with value?

constraints: Review and cleanup are part of the engineering work.
The goal is a faster, higher-quality end-to-end change process.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The measures require review labels and longer observation windows, but they prevent a high-volume generator from appearing productive while increasing cycle time.
details.errorCorrection: Replace activity counts with measures that include human correction and the business process outcome the assistant is meant to improve.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Outcome measures join model output to reviewer disposition and repository completion; a baseline comparison reveals whether assistance reduces total engineering effort.
details.scenarioApplication: Track accepted-change rate by task type and elapsed request-to-merge time including review and rework against a matched non-assistant baseline.
details.transfer: For AI-assisted work, measure what users accept and how long the complete job takes, not how much text the model emits.

messages.text: Suggestion volume rewards generation even when reviewers reject or rewrite the output and does not measure completed work.
Response length is not code quality or engineering productivity and can increase review burden.
Touched-file count can reflect noisy or harmful changes and has no relationship to accepted delivery time.
Without accepted-change rate, the team cannot tell whether generated suggestions are useful enough to keep.
Without end-to-end cycle time including review and rework, the dashboard can miss a productivity loss caused by cleanup.

feedback.reason: Accepted changes capture usefulness and cycle time captures the full productivity effect, including review and cleanup. Suggestion volume can rise while the process gets slower.

options.text: Accepted-change rate on representative suggestions, including the proportion merged with no substantive rewrite.
Total suggestions generated per developer, regardless of whether a change is accepted or useful.
Average response length, because longer code explanations indicate more capable assistance.
Number of files touched by each suggestion, even when reviewers revert the change.
End-to-end cycle time from request through review and rework to an accepted change, compared with the current workflow.

prompt: A coding assistant produces many suggestions, but reviewers reject a large share and cleanup extends the engineering cycle. Which TWO measures should replace suggestion volume as the primary value signal? Select TWO.
